sections.title: Automatic Sample Weight Transfer Explained
sections.tabSummary: What removing a manual data-entry step actually prevents
body: What removing a manual data-entry step actually prevents in a routine titration workflow.

A titration result is only as accurate as the sample weight it's calculated against, and manually typing that weight into the titrator introduces a genuine risk: a transposed digit, a missed decimal point, or simply the wrong sample's weight entered against the wrong run. That error doesn't show up as an obviously wrong result, it just quietly skews the calculation.
EasyPlus Easy pH's automatic sample weight transfer removes that step entirely, taking the weight directly from a connected balance rather than depending on the operator to type it in correctly.

body: What each of Easy Pro's three titration types actually determines, and why covering all three in one instrument matters.

Different sample parameters need fundamentally different titration chemistry: acid/base titration measures acidity or alkalinity, precipitation titration determines ions that form an insoluble compound with the titrant, such as chloride, and redox titration measures oxidation-reduction based parameters. A lab testing a varied product range often needs all three at different times, and running three separate single-method instruments for that is both more expensive and more bench space than the testing volume usually justifies.

Easy Pro consolidates all three into one instrument, so a food or chemical lab covering acidity, precipitation-based, and redox-based parameters doesn't need to own, calibrate, and maintain three separate titrators to do it.

sections.tabSummary: What the method actually measures, and why the range matters
body: What Easy KF V actually measures, and why the 100 ppm to 100% range matters.

Water content is one of the most common things a lab needs to verify, whether that's confirming a chemical is dry enough to use, checking a food product's moisture level, or verifying a raw material meets spec. Karl Fischer titration measures that directly and precisely, reacting the sample's water content with Karl Fischer reagent and calculating the exact amount present.

Easy KF V's 100 ppm to 100% range means the same instrument covers both trace-level moisture checks and samples that are mostly water, without needing a different method or instrument for each end of that range. Volumetric KF, as opposed to coulometric, is generally the right fit for the higher end of that range, where enough water is present to titrate directly.

sections.tabSummary: What growing from one burette to four, and adding InMotion, actually solves
body: What growing from one burette to four, and adding InMotion automation, actually solves for a lab whose testing needs change over time.

A lab buying its first titrator often doesn't know yet where its testing will be in two years, more sample types, more parallel methods, higher volume. Buying a fixed, single-burette instrument up front means a second purchase later if the testing grows, and buying a fully-loaded instrument up front means paying for capacity that may sit unused for years.

Excellence T5 sidesteps that choice: it starts as a single-burette titrator and expands up to four (one for titration, two more for dosing only) as the actual testing load grows, without replacing the instrument. InMotion or Rondolino automation layers on top of that, taking the same instrument from manual sample loading to running up to 303 samples per analysis without an operator present for each one.

sections.tabSummary: What 120,000 steps and a 0.2 mg LOQ actually mean for accuracy
body: What 120,000 dispensing steps and a 0.2 mg limit of quantification actually mean for the accuracy of a result.

A titrator's burette resolution determines how finely it can add reagent, and a coarser burette means a coarser titration curve, which shows up as noise in the final result, especially at low water levels where every increment matters. EVA V1's 120,000-step resolution gives it a genuinely fine dispensing curve, tested to DIN/ISO 8655-3 for accuracy and precision rather than just stated.

The limit of quantification, 0.2 mg water per sample at 1% RSD, is the practical consequence of that resolution: it's the smallest water content EVA V1 can reliably report with confidence, not just detect. For a lab testing genuinely low-moisture samples, that number matters more than almost any other spec on the sheet.

sections.title: Coulometric vs Volumetric Karl Fischer Explained
sections.tabSummary: Why EVA C1 reaches micrograms where EVA V1 works in milligrams
body: Why EVA C1 reaches micrograms of water where EVA V1's volumetric method works in milligrams.

Volumetric Karl Fischer titration adds a KF reagent of known concentration until the reaction with water completes, and the amount added tells you how much water was present, a method well suited to samples with a reasonable amount of water. Coulometric KF titration works differently: it generates the reactive iodine electrochemically, in situ, and measures the electric charge needed to do it, which lets it detect and quantify far smaller amounts of water with far greater sensitivity.

That's the difference between EVA V1's 100 ppm to 100% volumetric range and EVA C1's 0.01 to 200 mg coulometric range with a 2 µg detection limit: coulometric titration is built for exactly the trace end that volumetric titration isn't precise enough to reach reliably.
